summary.text: Deuterium, also called heavy hydrogen, is one of two stable isotopes of hydrogen, and its nucleus holds one proton and one neutron.
Nearly all the deuterium found in nature was made in the Big Bang, and stars destroy it in fusion reactions.
It is used in most nuclear weapons, many fusion power experiments, and as a neutron moderator in heavy water nuclear reactors.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: About twice that of ordinary hydrogen

facts.label: Nobel Prize
facts.value: Urey won it in 1934 for the discovery

facts.label: Primordial ratio
facts.value: About 26 deuterium nuclei per 10⁶ hydrogen nuclei

items.prompt: Ordinary hydrogen's nucleus has no neutrons. What does the nucleus of deuterium hold?

options.label: Two protons and no neutrons
One neutron and no protons
One proton and one neutron
Two neutrons and one proton

items.explain: The deuterium nucleus contains one proton and one neutron.

items.prompt: Stars burn hydrogen, yet nearly all the deuterium around us predates them. Why?

options.label: Stars destroy deuterium in fusion reactions
Stars cannot make any hydrogen isotope
Deuterium is too heavy to leave a star
Only planets can hold deuterium

items.explain: Synthesis during the formation of the universe is the only significant way natural deuterium was created, and it is destroyed in stellar fusion.

items.prompt: Right after the Big Bang it was so hot that newly formed deuterium was broken up at once. What did this hold up?

options.label: The cooling of the universe
The formation of free neutrons
The expansion of space
The building of helium-4

items.explain: Forming helium-4 requires deuterium as an intermediate step, so this deuterium bottleneck delayed helium-4 formation.

items.prompt: In heavy water nuclear reactors, deuterium does which job?

options.label: It is the fuel that gets split
It serves as the neutron moderator
It acts as a coolant gas
It coats the control rods

items.explain: Deuterium is used as the most effective neutron moderator, primarily in heavy water nuclear reactors.

items.prompt: A chemist running a hydrogen NMR scan dissolves a sample in a solvent where the hydrogen is replaced by deuterium. Why?

options.label: To make the scan run much faster overall
To make the whole sample heavier and steadier
So the solvent's signal stays off the sample's
To keep the sample cold while it is scanned

items.explain: Deuterated solvents are used in protium NMR to prevent the solvent from overlapping with the signal.

items.prompt: A heavier isotope of most elements acts almost like the lighter one, but deuterium differs more from ordinary hydrogen. Why?

options.label: It has twice as many electrons as hydrogen
It carries a strong electric charge
It is radioactive and slowly decays
It is about twice as massive as hydrogen

items.explain: Its large mass difference from protium confers non-negligible chemical differences, while isotope weight ratios in other elements are largely insignificant.

paragraphs.heading: Heavy hydrogen
paragraphs.text: Deuterium, written D or ²H and also called heavy hydrogen, is one of hydrogen's two stable isotopes. The other one is protium, or hydrogen-1, which is far more common. A deuterium nucleus, called a deuteron, holds one proton and one neutron, while protium has no neutrons at all. The name comes from the Greek word deuteros, meaning second.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery
paragraphs.text: The American chemist Harold Urey discovered deuterium in 1931. He and others made samples of heavy water in which deuterium was highly concentrated. The discovery earned Urey a Nobel Prize in 1934.

paragraphs.heading: Made in the Big Bang
paragraphs.text: Nearly all deuterium in nature was formed in the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago, leaving about 26 deuterium nuclei for every 10⁶ hydrogen nuclei. Stars make a little more through the slow proton–proton chain, but fusion reactions destroy it quickly. Making helium-4 requires forming deuterium first. In the first few minutes the universe was so hot that any deuterium that formed was broken apart straight away. This deuterium bottleneck held back helium-4 until the universe cooled enough for deuterium to survive, at a temperature equivalent to about 100 keV.

paragraphs.heading: A clue to Earth's oceans
paragraphs.text: The share of deuterium works like a fingerprint. Gas giant planets keep the primordial ratio. Comets show a higher ratio, similar to that of Earth's oceans at 156 deuterium nuclei per 10⁶ hydrogen nuclei, which supports the idea that much of the ocean's water came from comets. Yet the Rosetta probe found that comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko has about three times the ratio of Earth water, the highest measured in any comet so far.

paragraphs.heading: Twice the mass
paragraphs.text: A deuterium atom weighs 2.014102 Da, roughly double the mass of protium. Such a large mass difference gives deuterium compounds chemical differences from ¹H compounds that are not negligible. It also shifts light: every deuterium spectral line has a wavelength 0.0272% shorter than the matching line of light hydrogen. The differences are much larger in infrared, Raman and microwave spectra.

paragraphs.heading: What it is used for
paragraphs.text: Deuterium is used in most nuclear weapons and in many fusion power experiments. It is also the most effective neutron moderator, mainly in heavy water nuclear reactors. Scientists use it as an isotopic label, in biogeochemistry and in deuterated drugs. In NMR spectroscopy it has a very different frequency from protium, so deuterated solvents are usually used in protium NMR to keep the solvent from overlapping with the signal.
